source_text: Cum moneat Dominus et dicat: uos estis sal terrae cumque esse nos iubeat ad innocentiam simplices et tamen cum, simplicitate prudentes, quid aliud, fratres dilectissimi, quam prouidere nos conuenit et sollicito corde uigilantes subdoli hostis insidias intellegere pariter et cauere, ne qui Christum sapientiam Dei patris induimus minus sapere in tuenda salute uideamur? neque enim persecutio sola metuenda est et ea quae subruendis ac deiciendis semis Dei aperta inpugnatione grassantur, facilior cautio est ubi manifesta formido est, et ad certamen animus ante praestruitur, quando se aduersarius confitetur. plus timendus est et cauendus inimicus, cum latenter obrepit, cum per pacis imaginem fallens occultis accessibus serpit, unde et nomen serpentis accepit. ea est eius semper astutia, ea est circumueniendi hominis caeca et latebrosa fallacia. sic ab initio statim mundi fefellit et uerbis mendacibus blandiens rudem animam incauta credulitate decepit: sic dominum ipsum temptare conatus, quasi obreperet rursus et falleret, latenter accessit: intellectus tamen est et retusus et ideo prostratus quia agnitus adque detectus.
thought_title: The serpent's hidden attack is more to be feared than open persecution
orientation: Cyprian opens his treatise by addressing his beloved brethren, warning that the devil's hidden, deceptive attacks are more dangerous than open persecution.
pass_a_gloss: Since the Lord warns and says: 'You are the salt of the earth,' and since he commands us to be simple unto innocence and yet prudent with simplicity, what else, most beloved brethren, is fitting for us than to look ahead and, watching with anxious heart, to understand and likewise to avoid the snares of the crafty enemy, lest we who have put on Christ, the wisdom of God the Father, seem to have too little wisdom in guarding salvation? For persecution alone is not to be feared, and those things which rage in open attack for the overthrowing and casting down of the servants of God: the caution is easier where the fear is manifest, and the mind is prepared beforehand for the contest when the adversary declares himself. More to be feared and avoided is the enemy when he creeps up secretly, when, deceiving through the appearance of peace, he crawls near by hidden approaches, from which also he received the name of serpent. This is always his cunning, this is the blind and lurking deceit of circumventing man. Thus from the very beginning of the world he deceived, and, flattering with lying words, he tricked the inexperienced soul with incautious credulity: thus, attempting to tempt the Lord himself, as if he would creep up again and deceive, he approached secretly: nevertheless he was recognized and repulsed, and therefore cast down because he was recognized and detected.

choices.why: Direct quotation from Matthew 5:13; kept literal as the familiar biblical phrase.
Preserves the Latin construction with 'ad' expressing purpose or result, matching the moral sense of simplicity directed toward innocence.
Keeps the ablative of quality and the contrast between simplicity and prudence, echoing Matthew 10:16.
'Subdolus' means deceitful or crafty; 'hostis' is enemy, here the devil. Literal rendering preserves the characterization.

choices.english: deceiving through the appearance of peace
choices.why: 'Imago' is appearance or semblance; the phrase captures the devil's deceptive pretense of peace.
rejected: by a false show of peace

choices.why: 'Caeca' is blind, 'latebrosa' means full of hiding places or lurking; both adjectives describe the hidden nature of the deceit.

bible_refs.note: simplices ... prudentes, echoing 'be wise as serpents and innocent as doves'

pass_b_english: The Lord warns us and says, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13), and he commands us to be simple unto innocence, yet prudent with simplicity. So what else, dearly beloved brothers, should we do but look ahead, and with watchful hearts stay alert, so that we both understand and avoid the snares of the crafty enemy? For we have put on Christ, the wisdom of God the Father, and we must not seem to lack wisdom in guarding our salvation. Persecution alone is not what we must fear, nor the attacks that rage openly to overthrow and cast down the servants of God. Caution is easier where the danger is plain, and the mind is prepared for battle beforehand when the adversary admits who he is. The enemy we must fear and guard against more is the one who creeps up secretly, who deceives through the appearance of peace and crawls near by hidden approaches. That is where he got the name “serpent.” This is always his cunning; this is the blind and lurking deceit by which he traps a person. So from the very beginning of the world he deceived, flattering the untried soul with lying words and catching it by careless trust. So too he tried to tempt the Lord himself, approaching secretly as if he could creep up and deceive him again. But he was recognized and repulsed, and therefore thrown down, because he was known and exposed.

last_rejected.quote: The Lord warns us and says
last_rejected.why: English hides that Cyprian is the speaker introducing Christ's words.
last_rejected.ruling: Cum + subjunctive introduces background; English captures it fine. No speaker confusion.

last_rejected.why: Wrong sense: 'ad innocentiam' means 'toward innocence,' not 'unto innocence.'
last_rejected.ruling: 'Unto' and 'toward' both render 'ad'; no meaning change.

last_rejected.why: Ablative means 'prudent in simplicity,' not 'with simplicity' as accompaniment.
last_rejected.ruling: 'With simplicity' is normal rendering of ablative; no meaning change.

last_rejected.why: 'Prouidere' here means 'take forethought/provide for,' not merely 'look ahead.'
last_rejected.ruling: 'Look ahead' is within 'prouidere' range; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: we must not seem to lack wisdom
last_rejected.source_quote: minus sapere in tuenda salute uideamur
last_rejected.why: Flipped meaning: 'minus sapere' is 'be less wise,' not 'lack wisdom' absolutely.
last_rejected.fix: we must not seem less wise in guarding our salvation
last_rejected.ruling: 'Lack wisdom' captures 'minus sapere' adequately; no real meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: Persecution alone is not what we must fear
last_rejected.source_quote: neque enim persecutio sola metuenda est
last_rejected.why: Wrong emphasis: 'sola' modifies 'persecutio,' meaning 'persecution alone is not to be feared,' i.e., not only persecution.
last_rejected.fix: Persecution is not the only thing to be feared
last_rejected.ruling: 'Persecution alone is not what we must fear' matches 'persecutio sola metuenda est' correctly.

last_rejected.quote: Caution is easier where the danger is plain
last_rejected.source_quote: facilior cautio est ubi manifesta formido est
last_rejected.why: Missing comparative: 'facilior' means 'easier,' but English loses the implicit contrast with hidden danger.
last_rejected.fix: Caution is easier when the danger is out in the open
last_rejected.ruling: 'Easier' preserves comparative; implicit contrast is clear from context.

last_rejected.quote: the mind is prepared for battle beforehand
last_rejected.fix: the mind is fortified for battle in advance
last_rejected.ruling: 'Prepared' is within 'praestruitur' range; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: when the adversary admits who he is
last_rejected.why: 'Confess' here means 'acknowledges/reveals himself,' not 'admits who he is' with identity sense.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Admits who he is' captures 'se confitetur' adequately; no meaning change.

last_rejected.why: 'Homo' here is generic 'human being,' but 'circumuenire' means 'to circumvent/ensnare/entrap.'
last_rejected.ruling: 'Traps a person' renders 'circumueniendi hominis' correctly; mere preference only.
'Untried' is within 'rudis' range; no misleading change.
'Careless trust' captures 'incauta credulitate' adequately; no real error.
